title: TROLL: Trust Regions Improve Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
claim: A projection keeps the updated policy inside a principled trust region, and this yields faster, higher-performing training than heuristic clipping.
layout: 3 panels: simplex sketch left, two line plots right; emoji vertices as device
description: The figure has two halves. On the left, a large triangle (probability simplex) has a cat emoji at the bottom-left corner, a hamster at the bottom-right and a troll at the top. A blue gradient is centred on a red diamond, which marks the old policy. A black oval around the diamond marks the trust region. A green curve leads from the oval's boundary to a blue diamond near the hamster corner. The green diamond on the boundary marks the projected policy. A legend at top-left explains the red, blue and green markers with policy notation. On the right, two line plots show mean success rate against wallclock time in hours, one for MATH and one for Eurus-Code. A solid dark-teal TROLL curve sits clearly above a dashed Clip curve in both. Faint raw traces sit behind the smoothed lines.
caption: \gls{troll} overview. (Left) Example of a 3-token distribution (cat, troll, hamster). The old policy favors the troll, while the new policy shifts toward the hamster. The projection ensures that the updated policy stays within the trust region (circle). (Right) \gls{troll} yields clear performance gains over PPO-like clipping (CLIP) on mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, as shown for Qwen3-14B trained with GRPO.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) with PPO-like clip objectives has become the standard choice for reward-based fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Although recent work has explored improved estimators of advantages and normalization, the clipping mechanism itself has remained untouched. Originally introduced as a proxy for principled KL-based trust regions, clipping is a crude approximation that often causes unstable updates and suboptimal performance. We replace the clip objective with a novel discrete differentiable trust region projection, which provides principled token-level KL constraints. The projection operates on a sparse subset of the model's most important token logits to balance computational cost and projection effectiveness. Our approach, Trust Region Optimization for Large Language models (TROLL), serves as a direct replacement for PPO-like clipping during training and does not alter the model's inference behavior. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, model families, as well as advantage-estimation methods, TROLL consistently outperforms PPO-like clipping in terms of training speed, stability, and final success rates.
